opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea behind Voyager is that we wanted an agent that keeps getting better on its own, the way a human player does when they drop into Minecraft with no manual. The trick is that we don't represent skills as neural network weights. We represent them as code.

When Voyager figures out how to do something, like crafting a stone pickaxe or fighting a zombie, it writes a JavaScript program against the Minecraft API. Once that program has been verified to actually work in the environment, we store it in what we call a skill library. Each skill is indexed by an embedding of its description, so later, when the agent faces a new task, it can retrieve the relevant skills and compose them into something more complex. Simple skills become building blocks for harder ones. "Mine wood" feeds into "craft planks," which feeds into "make a crafting table," and so on up the tech tree.

There are really three pieces working together. First, an automatic curriculum: GPT-4 looks at the agent's current state and inventory and proposes the next task that's challenging but achievable. It's basically novelty-seeking, always pushing the frontier of exploration. Second, the skill library I just described. And third, an iterative prompting loop. The agent writes code, runs it, and gets feedback: execution errors, environment observations, and a self-verification check where another model call judges whether the task actually succeeded. It keeps refining until the skill works, and only then does it get committed to the library.

What I find most exciting is that this sidesteps catastrophic forgetting. In standard reinforcement learning, learning a new skill can overwrite an old one in the weights. Code doesn't have that problem. It's interpretable, it's compositional, and it's temporally extended, so one function can encode a long sequence of actions. And because the library is just code, you can take it to a brand-new Minecraft world and the agent can solve novel tasks zero-shot, which we showed in the paper.

The bigger lesson for me is that the language model acts as a kind of blind but very knowledgeable reasoner, and code becomes the action space that grounds it. It's a form of lifelong learning where we never do any gradient updates. All the "learning" happens in the growing library and in context. I think that's a pattern we'll see much more of in embodied agents going forward, even as we move toward physical robots, where the analogous building blocks might be motor skills rather than JavaScript functions.

r001.rationale: It says the agent runs its code, gets execution errors and observations, and keeps refining it until the skill works.

r002.rationale: It identifies a skill as a JavaScript program that Voyager has verified works in the environment.

r003.rationale: It says Voyager retrieves relevant skills for later tasks, but does not clearly explain that retrieval avoids repeating trial-and-error programming in a similar situation.

r004.rationale: It says Voyager writes the programs itself and stores them in a library of code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Voyager is really my favorite example of what I'd call a lifelong learning agent, and the key insight is that we don't do any gradient updates at all. The language model is frozen. What's learning is a library of code.

So the way it works is, Voyager gets a text description of what it's seeing in Minecraft, the inventory, the biome, nearby blocks, and so on. And then it writes code, JavaScript against the Mineflayer API, to do something like, say, craft a wooden pickaxe. That program is the skill. If it runs and succeeds, we store it in a skill library. If it fails, we feed the error message, or the game feedback like "you don't have enough wood," back into the model, and it iterates, basically debugging itself. That's the self-reflection loop.

And the reason the skill library matters so much is that code composes. Once you have "chop a tree" as a function, "craft a wooden pickaxe" can call it. Once you have the pickaxe, "mine iron" builds on top of that. So skills become building blocks for more complex skills, and the agent is essentially bootstrapping a tech tree out of its own past experience. We retrieve skills by embedding the description of the task and pulling the most relevant programs out of the library, so you get this interpretable, growing memory that isn't locked inside the weights.

The other piece is the automatic curriculum. We don't tell Voyager what to do. We ask the model, given everything you've done so far and what's around you, what's the next interesting and achievable thing? And because it's trained on the internet, it kind of knows the Minecraft progression. Wood, then stone, then iron, then diamond. So it proposes tasks that are just at the edge of its current abilities, and that keeps exploration going without us hand-designing a reward function.

What I find most exciting is that the skills transfer. You can drop Voyager into a brand new world with a fresh map, give it the library it learned before, and it solves new tasks much faster. That's something you basically never get from classical RL on Minecraft, where the policy is this opaque thing tied to the pixels of one environment. Here the knowledge is in a form humans can read, edit, and reuse, which I think is a glimpse of how agents in general, not just in games, might accumulate competence over time.

r001.rationale: It says failed code receives error or game feedback and Voyager iterates by debugging the code.

r002.rationale: It defines a skill as code that is stored when it runs successfully.

r003.rationale: It says Voyager retrieves relevant stored programs and builds skills on one another, but does not clearly state that retrieval avoids repeating trial-and-error programming in a similar situation.

r004.rationale: It describes Voyager writing code itself and accumulating successful programs in its skill library.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about Voyager is that it’s building a library of things it knows how to do. As it explores Minecraft, it sets a goal, writes code to accomplish that goal, and then uses feedback from the environment to improve the code. If something fails, that failure becomes information for the next attempt.

The key is that a successful behavior doesn’t just disappear at the end of the interaction. Voyager can save it as a reusable skill. So when it encounters a more complex task, it can retrieve skills it has already learned and compose them, instead of figuring everything out from scratch.

That gives you this compounding effect: better skills let it explore more of the world, and exploring more of the world creates opportunities to learn new skills. In that sense, the skill library is a kind of persistent memory, expressed as executable code.

r001.rationale: It says Voyager uses environmental feedback and failures to improve the code it wrote.

r002.rationale: It describes successful behavior as a reusable skill and says the skill library is expressed as executable code, linking skills to working programs.

r003.rationale: It says Voyager retrieves learned skills for more complex tasks and composes them instead of figuring everything out from scratch, conveying that it avoids repeating the learning process.

r004.rationale: It describes Voyager setting goals and writing code during exploration, then saving successful behaviors into a library of executable skills, characterizing the library as agent-authored code.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about Voyager is that it builds up a library of things it knows how to do. In Minecraft, you don’t want the agent to figure out how to craft a pickaxe from scratch every time it needs one. Once it solves that problem, it can save the solution as a piece of code and reuse it later.

There’s a feedback loop behind that. The agent proposes a task, writes code to carry it out, executes that code, and looks at what happened. If it fails, it can use the error messages and observations from the environment to revise its approach. When it succeeds, that behavior becomes a reusable skill.

And those skills can compose. Gathering materials supports crafting tools, which supports mining new resources, which opens up more tasks. So the interesting thing is that the agent’s capabilities can keep growing through interaction, even though the underlying language model’s weights aren’t changing. The skill library becomes a kind of persistent memory of what it has learned to do.

r001.rationale: It says the agent executes its code, uses errors and observations from the environment, and revises its approach when it fails.

r002.rationale: It describes saving a solved task as code and says successful behavior becomes a reusable skill.

r003.rationale: It says the agent can reuse a saved solution instead of figuring out how to craft a pickaxe from scratch each time.

r004.rationale: It says the agent writes code and builds a library of reusable skills from that code, communicating that the library is authored by the agent.
